text: Any couple who has been married for several years will share that it requires much effort by both parties to make a marriage work.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even for happy marriages, there will always be the inevitable quarrels or disputes over finances, lifestyle, upbringing of children and even relationship issues involving the in-laws.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a written response by the National Council of Churches of Singapore (NCCS) in June last year, NCCS expressed concern that “some couples may see the amicable divorce option as providing an easy exit that will allow them to run away from their problems without having to assign blame.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, instead of trying to find solutions to their problems as a couple that have pledged their lifelong commitment to each other, that husband or wife may simply decide to end their marriage.” Sir, I share the same concern as NCCS.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I recognise that, sometimes, despite the best efforts, marriages do not work out for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In such cases, the law should allow couples to exit from an unhappy marriage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The current laws recognise that when marriages do not work, parties can file for divorce because the marriage has broken down irretrievably.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Currently, there are five possible grounds which constitute irretrievable breakdown of marriage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Three of these grounds are what divorce lawyers commonly call “fault” divorces: adultery, unreasonable behaviour and desertion for a period of two years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are factors causing the irretrievable breakdown in marriage: a party's adultery, a party's unreasonable behaviour or a party's desertion.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The other two grounds are what we call “no fault” divorces which are based on separation for a period of three years with consent or separation for four years even without consent.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is the period of living separate and apart which causes the marriage to breakdown.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some Members of this House may recall that in the 1970s, parties applying for divorce based on separation were required to live separate and apart for an even longer period of seven years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, over these years, there have been changes to make divorce easier by shortening the separation period.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, in actual fact, parties can divorce without apportioning fault, except that they need to wait the statutory period of three years or four years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In 2015, the Courts had introduced the Simplified Track for divorce where parties who are able to agree on the terms of divorce and the ancillary matters can have their divorce application dealt with expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, for parties who wish to settle their divorce cases quickly, the Simplified Track divorce is already an option where parties have to be less acrimonious if they want their divorce to proceed smoothly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They still need to cite one of the five grounds when they file for the divorce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But most parties will come to a compromise on the grounds of divorce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For cases where parties are unable to agree and wish to contest the divorce, the Courts would, usually, call both parties down for what we call a status conference where the judge would invite parties to review their position whether to have an acrimonious contested divorce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Frequently, both parties will, eventually, accept that if the marriage has broken down, then a contested divorce will not serve anyone’s interest.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is because, within a divorce, it basically means that the parties remain married, even though they have undergone a contentious divorce hearing, and that does not make sense.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And the year before, there were 7,623 divorces, with 25,434 marriages.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What is the change in circumstances that triggered the need for the introduction of this provision?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Does the Government not acknowledge that a divorce may have serious consequences for the children?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some years back, MCCY, as it then was, used to produce pamphlets on divorce: "Before you Divorce", "Divorce" and "How to Survive Children and Divorce".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And these pamphlets highlighted the real issues about divorce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One particular pamphlet stood out to me – this is it, for Members of the House who are interested – and this pamphlet says: “At some time in a marriage, problems will arise.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of these problems seem intractable, others do not.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the problems that seem intractable, people often think that divorce is the answer." And it concluded with the words "Think Again". "Think Again".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, this pamphlet is available to parties who wanted to file for divorce at the time and it really urged couples thinking of divorce to "Think Again".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A vow to commit to a marriage can now simply be revoked by mutual agreement to divorce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Has the Government made any study of the experience in other countries which allow divorce by mutual consent?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would allowing DMA result in an increase in divorce rates?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What if this amendment does, in actual fact, result in divorce applications going up by a large number in the next few years?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How would the Government then try to arrest the increase in divorce numbers because it may be impossible to turn back the change?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When parties have to cite the reasons for concluding that the marriage has broken down irretrievably, it will be inevitable that there would be some accusations against the other.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also hope that the Government is cognisant that DMA does not mean that there will not be acrimonious litigation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Parties could still fight tooth and nail regarding custody, care and control over the children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They will still fight over the division of assets and maintenance.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sadly, Sir, divorce is a very emotional process where parties frequently feel betrayed and the acrimony is always there.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, where parties acknowledge that no one is at fault but they nevertheless want a divorce due to incompatibility or for whatever reason, the advice that can be given to them is to live separate and apart and meet the legal criteria for divorce based on three years or four years separation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, parties may want a divorce due to misunderstandings, failure to communicate, quarrels over issues which they feel emotional about.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In situations like these, separation may allow parties time to cool down, to review their reasons for wanting a divorce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That separation may not always lead to reconciliation between the parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But a divorce does have a massive impact on the parties, especially when young children are involved.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If parties are open to attending marital counselling during the separation to help them work out their differences, sometimes, the marriage may be salvaged.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We can do more to build up the institution of marriage in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As someone who is newly married, of course, my hope is that it does not end in divorce.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Before my marriage, I also attended a pre-marriage course in the hopes that it would prepare me better for the greater responsibilities that would come.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I do acknowledge that marriage may sometimes fail despite the best efforts from both parties.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There are worries on whether it will make the divorce process easier.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: On the contrary, the current safeguards, such as having to be married for at least three years before filing for divorce, as well as a three-month period before the divorce is finalised, are there.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, couples will have to show that they have tried to reconcile and the efforts they have made to settle their children and financial affairs after their divorce.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Court is also able to reject the couple's application if it is deemed that reconciliation is possible.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Such couples will have to go through further mediation and counselling.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, this also aims to protect the children's interests.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: By not needing to state the fault of a divorce and to prove or disprove allegations and thereby causing further tensions, children may be spared the trauma of such experiences.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Divorce may have a traumatising effect on all parties involved, especially children, and even then, not just those in the immediate family.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This step allows families to be better supported throughout the whole process, placing importance on their mental well-being and, hopefully, ensuring that the divorce process has a reduced impact on other aspects of their lives.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: All in all, I do believe that the underlying intention is to strengthen marriages and to mitigate the negative effects of divorce and, for that, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The institution of marriage is one of the oldest practices that has been established since the birth of human civilisation, yet the notion of romantic love as the motivating force for marriage only goes as far back as the Middle Ages and the American and French revolutions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But for much of human history prior, couples were brought together for practical reasons and not because they fell in love.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even in the 20th century and within our very own Pioneer Generation, arranged marriages were not an uncommon theme among Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, on reflection, it seems that our understanding and experience of romantic marriages are of a much lesser degree and, consequently, our principles and laws governing such marriages, likewise, see a need for finetuning and revision.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a marriage founded on love, self-fulfilment and companionship, it becomes plausible that a marriage could cease when individuals fall out of love or if ones' needs and expectations are not met in a marriage – the former cannot exist without the latter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a society, we strive to nurture and preserve the sacred union of a couple.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To make the decision to terminate an unsatisfying marriage signifies a major turning point in an individual's life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I can only imagine the major turbulences and disorientations one might experience being thrust out of their comfort zones and being confronted with intense uncertainty and inconsistency.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Along with the heavy emotional distress and anxiety one faces during the different points of one's divorce journey, individuals going through a divorce are also faced with many tangible and financial issues, often expected to single-handedly formulate ways to deal with post-divorce adjustments in areas of housing and childcare.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These struggles were made real to me when I came across the personal stories of my constituents, some of whom had felt much loneliness and despair when it came to the dissolution of their marriages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of my constituents came out of a troubled, abusive marriage and faced immense difficulty as she had to find the balance taking care of her two young children, who were traumatised by their parents' difficult relationship, and looking for a job as she sought to provide for her children and family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many other constituents have come to look for me for help with their housing after their marriages were dissolved, marital homes sold and they and their children unceremoniously faced with worries about having no roofs over their heads.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many a time, my divorced female constituents have no savings, have not been in formal employment for a while and are facing the complex conundrum of securing a job, finding the financials to purchase a new family home, securing the well-being of their children and also tending to their raw feelings of a dissolved marriage.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the early stages of parenthood, the ability to financially support one's family is often of immediate and significant importance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement has recognised a need to provide support in this area.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our union leaders – both men and women – have frequently voiced the need to extend employment support for single mothers who require help securing jobs after a divorce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC Women and Family (WAF) unit also works with the larger Labour Movement Family, such as NTUC's SME unit, to promote flexi-work arrangements and work-life harmony practices that support women in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Earlier this year, the Women and Family unit also piloted the Women Supporting Women mentorship to unite women union and grassroot leaders to provide career guidance and advice to women in the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through this programme and the networks of our union leaders, many single mothers have been able to connect with job opportunities and build up their confidence of coming back to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although these efforts have been made, our experience with newly-single mothers reflects the need to continue striving to provide support for single mothers as they navigate a new chapter in their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many single mothers have also told me that they would love greater work flexibility to allow them time to send their children to and fro from school.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Providing these networks allows for divorced mothers greater assurance that their family is taken care of and, in turn, granting them peace of mind to maximise what they do in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today, marriage is no longer a matter between two families, but a relationship built on the foundation of love between two persons.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in the past, most marriages were arranged by parents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Chinese used to say that marriage is by the order of parents and the words of the matchmaker, and that married women are like water poured away.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because of this thinking, many women are aggrieved in the process of divorce or suffer in life after divorce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must not turn a blind eye to these problems.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When a woman is dragged down by an unsuitable or even unsafe marriage and ends up in divorce, it is not difficult for us to imagine the physical and mental sufferings that decades of ups and downs can bring to her.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Financial issues, social discrimination, bread-and-butter issues and children’s education will come in tandem.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We do not know if a marriage or divorce is a path apart or a rebirth, but our laws can support these women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): If marriage is seen as one of life's major milestones, then a divorce and its proceedings should be accorded the same, if not greater understanding.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although divorce may bring about unfavourable repercussions, such a choice should not result in lifelong calamity but rather a fresh start and new beginnings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The provision of livelihood options and its surrounding support mechanisms, such as caregiving support to divorced women and parents, are an important key to this fresh start.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Marriage is a lifelong commitment between two individuals who intend to be in a legally-binding union and share a life together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the guiding principle has always been that family is the first line of care and support.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, policy and legislative amendments relating to marriages and marital dissolutions can have a deep impact on our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I would like to focus my speech on raising three considerations on the Women's Charter (Amendment) Bill to ensure: one, civil marriages will continue to be upheld and conducted with solemnity; and, two, women and children will be protected in the event of a divorce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, new provisions will be included in the amendment to allow for the pre-solemnisation process to be completed online.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am supportive of MSF's wider effort to promote the digitalisation and enhancement of convenience of the marriage process.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I am concerned that virtual solemnisation might dilute the significance of marriages.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the lives of many newlyweds, solemnisation is an important ceremony for family members to witness and be part of the joy in celebrating their union together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An example of diluted significance of marriages for the purpose of convenience can be found in Nevada, United States.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Las Vegas, in the city of Nevada, is known to have a booming wedding industry.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Wedding-related tourism accounts for nearly US$2 billion of the city's annual US$58 billion tourism industry and generates about 18,000 jobs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the reasons for its booming industry is the convenience to get married, such as drive-through wedding services and 24-hour chapels to solemnise couples.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the amendment, the new section 95(3) stated that a Court "must dismiss an application if it is not satisfied that the marriage has irretrievably broken down and there remains a reasonable possibility that the parties might reconcile".

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There could, however, be situations where a spouse, who has higher financial control and power over the other, coerces the dependant spouse into mutual agreement to divorce but not out of that spouse's own will.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such situations, how will the Court be able to determine if the mutual agreement of the irretrievable breakdown of the marriage may not be out of their own volition of one of the parties?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there any safeguards that MSF will make to recommend to the Court that the marriage is still reconcilable?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, the Women Charter is also amended to mandate for all divorcing parents with minor children to attend the Mandatory Parenting Programme (MPP) before they can file for divorce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my interactions with residents who are going through divorces, they often share the emotional difficulties that they faced during the proceedings and worry about the impact that their divorce has on their children, especially when the other party refuses to cooperate and allow for a smooth divorce process.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a resident who once sought my help and shared with me how her ex-husband was missing through most part of the divorce proceedings and was only contactable before the final judgment for divorce is delivered by the Court.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such cases where the marriage has become acrimonious and one of the parties refuses to attend MPP to proceed with the divorce proceedings, will the other half be stuck in the marriage and unable to move on?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask what happens if the couple is going through a family violence situation and the perpetrator is not willing to attend MPP?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can MSF ensure that the divorce proceedings will continue and the victim can receive closure to move on in life?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As far as possible, conditions need to be created to allow couples to reconcile amid family disputes and marriage breakdowns.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is inevitable that divorces can occur and families possibly broken apart.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is my belief that there must then be therapeutic justice incorporated in divorce proceedings, in which acrimony and hostility during these proceedings would not be aggravated and the children's best interest is prioritised.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although couples can no longer be husbands and wives, they continue to be parents and role models for their children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, it is important that the amendments to the Women's Charter allow couples to have closure and move on with their separate lives, while continuing to be the pillar of support for the children that they would likely have to raise jointly.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I do stand in support of this Bill and welcome the amendments to better support our children and families undergoing divorce proceedings in our family justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: My speech will be focused on two areas: first, on children and family support programmes; and second, on child access orders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I welcome the changes which focus on the best interests of the child of the marriage and place importance on therapeutic justice and counselling as steps in the right direction to prevent acrimonious and protracted litigation which may cause greater divisions and rifts in relationships between parents and child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The children and family support programmes, including counselling, that are envisaged in these amendments would assist with the emotional aspects of dealing with the outcome of orders, particularly in cases involving the relocation of a child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: However, this is something that is not unfamiliar or new within the Family Justice System and I draw the experience and lessons from the Administration of Muslim Law Act amendments back in 2017 and the practice of the Syariah Court in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: (In Malay):   In early 2017, MCCY sought public feedback on the Administration of Muslim Law Act (AMLA) amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Various community groups provided their views and recommendations, including AMP, which, through RIMA, conducted a focus group discussion (FGD) to collate feedback among various stakeholders and interested individuals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The AMLA amendments at that time, among other things, firstly, enshrined a more “child-centric” approach during proceedings and allowed the Courts to refer parties for counselling or a family support programme.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Registration for the Marriage Counselling Programme must be submitted at the Syariah Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Pursuant to section 46A of AMLA, couples who are contemplating divorce are required to attend and complete the Marriage Counselling Programme.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The objective of the Marriage Counselling Programme is to assist the couples to explore reconciliation and, if the marriage cannot be saved, the counsellors will facilitate an amicable divorce instead.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Marriage Counselling Programme will be conducted by an agency appointed by the Syariah Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This is to make the divorce process less adversarial and help parties to consider the children’s interests and welfare when making decisions that will inevitably affect their children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: It also equips them with healthy co-parenting and self-care strategies and provide information on available support resources.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: These are the mandatory programmes within the divorce process before the Syariah Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Additionally, if parties have a child aged between six and 14, they are encouraged to attend the Children-in-Between programme with their child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This programme is free and conducted by the Divorce Support Specialist Agencies which are appointed by MSF.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: It aims to equip parents with co-parenting skills to promote parental cooperation so as to reduce harmful parental conflicts that are likely to have adverse effects on their child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The programme is also aimed at helping their child to be equipped with self-coping skills to help him or her cope with any stress and deal with the impact of the divorce.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Although the Children-in-Between programme is voluntary, where necessary, the Syariah Court may order parties and their child to attend the programme during or after the divorce proceedings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In summary, while the current amendments that we are debating today do not impact the divorce proceedings in the Syariah Court, from the Syariah Court's lessons and experience and from past amendments, it is a good step to make children-centric programmes and counselling part and parcel of our family justice process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: As such, I welcome the amendments to the Women’s Charter presently.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, with this, I have some clarifications In relation to divorces under the Family Justice Courts (FJCs), what is the rationale for not making the child's completion of a programme for children mandatory?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I ask this because it is already mandatory under section 50(3A) of the Women's Charter that divorcing parents with any child below 21 have to attend counselling or mediation sessions at the FJCs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The 2020 data also shows that couples who were married for five to nine years accounted for the largest share, 29.4%, of all divorces.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This is the same for both civil and Muslim divorces.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: There is, thus, a great likelihood that this segment of couples would have younger children as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: As such, these children may benefit from attending such programmes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I, thus, make two proposals in this regard which are akin to the Syariah Court experience that I have shared earlier.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This may nip in the bud any acrimonious or protracted divorce litigation which may be detrimental to the children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In relation to the programmes for children, the proposed new section 132A defines "programmes for children" as any programme carried out to help a child handle the impact of a divorce or judicial separation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Can the Minister perhaps provide examples, with reference to already existing programmes?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, I also make two separate proposals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Given the utility of such programmes and the need to develop human capital with the necessary expertise, perhaps a national professional body can be tasked to oversee training and provide such programmes across the board.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This facilitates harmonisation and uniform standards of counselling and the building up of cross-training, sharing of expertise and experiences for cases between both FJC and SYC.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This is useful, especially in cases of inter-faith or inter-ethnic marriages, where, apart from the parties, that is, the parents or the children, the prescribed persons like the grandparents or other caregivers may also come from different backgrounds, faiths or cultures.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: A second proposal perhaps is for greater collaboration and cooperation within the law schools, Law Society of Singapore and lawyers to inculcate, within the Bar, the importance of therapeutic justice and a child-centric approach towards divorces in our family justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In respect of access orders, I welcome the amendments to help expand the Court's enforcement powers in relation to custody orders and child access orders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has, inevitably, impacted custodial rights over children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: We have seen how the parent with care and control decided to unilaterally suspend, halt or restrict the other parent's visitation rights during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I have some concerns, however, on the amendments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Under the new section 126A, the Court is empowered to direct the bailiff to restore a child to the physical custody of a parent or other person.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Such order or direction, I think, should be used sparingly and reserved for the most egregious of cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: For example, where access orders have been breached on numerous occasions or where, despite the wishes of the child, the parent refused to give access to the other parent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: For young children, the experience of being taken, whether forcibly or otherwise, from the physical custody of one person to another, can be very traumatic.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, I have a few questions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: What are the guidelines and safeguards to ensure the safety and prevention of trauma on the child during the exercise of such powers?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Would the relevant officers and agencies also be trained to be more trauma-informed and sensitive to such situations?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Next, under the new section 126B, the Court has powers to enforce a child access order, including ordering make-up access and imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: If I may ask the Minister, in respect of make-up access orders, would this be determined with the best interest of the child in mind, before such orders are made?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I ask this because there may be other limitations, such as the child's other commitments and her or his own rest periods.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, usually, such breaching parent is the one with the care and control of the child.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Hence, would not a jail term be effectively disruptive to the care of the child?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In such an instance, who would take care of the child and who would effectively have care and control then?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications and proposals, Mr Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When a child is involved, it could get even harder.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Going through a divorce is an emotionally draining period and we should do our best to help fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should make sure our policies do not make the divorce process more acrimonious.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposed amendments to the Women's Charter are a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They modernise our marriage processes, allow for no-fault divorces and expand divorce support programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They acknowledge the reality that marriage, despite our best hopes and efforts, may break down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In such situations, our laws should help everyone affected, especially the children, to move on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope we can do more, much more, and I have three suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first suggestion is with regard to parents with shared care and control.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Couples know that if they get shared care and control of their child, they will have to fight each other for who gets to list their child as occupiers in their application for a HDB flat; essentially, who gets subsidised public housing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If one party gets sole care and control, then he or she is guaranteed this subsidised housing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is it in the best interest of the child for their parents to have a more acrimonious divorce?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We know that having a roof over one's head is essential and is perhaps one of the biggest worries following a divorce, especially for the lower income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As mentioned, HDB requires such parents to obtain mutual consent from the other parent before listing their child as an occupier in an HDB flat application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This creates three problems, all of which are bad for the children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, during divorce proceedings, parents may fight more aggressively for sole care and control to secure their right to apply for a subsidised HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, after divorce, parents may continue fighting over this issue of mutual consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, when one parent refuses to grant consent, the other parent and their child may be stuck in housing instability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This affects the child's material and emotional well-being.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But allowing appeals does not solve any of the above three problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our policies may still create tension, conflict and instability as a default for children in such cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three proposals for fixing this policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, the Ministry should work with the Family Courts to enable the Courts to settle the question of mutual consent at the stage of divorce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If both parents reach an agreement, it should be stated in the Matrimonial Property Plan and reflected in the divorce judgment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If they do not, each parent should present their reasons to the judge, who can make an order on which parent gets to list the child as an occupier.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not overly intrusive, as judges already settle property matters during divorce proceedings, such as by dividing the matrimonial property.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Divorce rulings also already decide on custody, care and control and division of matrimonial assets, which are equally contentious.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, HDB should drop its requirement for mutual consent as long as the other parent already owns private property.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, HDB should automatically allow parents to list the child as an occupier if both parents are of lower income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These proposals will help avoid adding housing instability to the children of divorced parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second suggestion is about the "Children-in-Between" programme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past few years, many people undergoing divorce have approached me for help, and many are in tears as they share their painful journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Often, I see their child, at times, a very young child, hugging their parents, comforting them and providing tissues to wipe their tears.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The children step up, but I often wonder if they truly understand what is happening to mummy and daddy and whether we are providing them with enough help during this very confusing, painful and distressing period for someone who is so young.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should do a lot more to make this number as close to 100% as possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final suggestion is about renaming the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When the Women's Charter was enacted in 1961, it was instrumental in protecting the rights of women.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today's amendments ensure that the Charter continues to do so, including by clarifying the rights and duties of husbands and wives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we modernise this law, we should also consider making its name more appropriate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My proposal is that we rename it to the Family Charter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, the bulk of this law protects not just women but men and children as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is also true of today's amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: No-fault divorces, children support programmes and modernised marriage solemnisations are all good not just for women but also for families in general.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, bundling family- and children-specific laws under a Women's Charter has the unintentional effect of suggesting that women have some unique place in raising children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It runs against everything else this Government is saying that men need to contribute equally at home, that employers should not treat women and mothers differently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know the Government does not mean to send this message, but that is what it looks like.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is bad for women, and it is bad for families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, there is a rising, incorrect sentiment that the Women's Charter is bad for men.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But renaming the Women's Charter to accurately describe its scope can help defuse the anger.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Renaming the Women's Charter does not mean we have achieved the goal of gender equality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data and stories make clear that there is still a painful inequality in everything, from attitudes to affluence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, marriage and divorce laws ought to be updated accordingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the new no-fault divorce policy, we follow in the footsteps of countries like Australia, Canada, China and Sweden.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: England and Wales will also adopt this no-fault approach this coming April.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This approach is increasingly advocated due to the widespread consensus that a contentious divorce has grave negative implications on children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In serious cases, it causes post-traumatic stress disorder.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Subsequently, when no blame is ascribed, parties involved in the divorce can also move on with their lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite its growing prevalence, no-fault divorce remains controversial.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is largely attributed to the common belief among naysayers that it will erode the sanctity of marriage and lead to a breakdown of the family unit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Considering this, I wish to raise three issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Government must ensure that the no-fault divorce policy will not be misconstrued as an easy way out of an unfulfilling marriage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry has also shared about the safeguards in place to prevent this from happening.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When vows are exchanged, couples look forward to spending the rest of their lives with their partners.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For at least one party in a marriage to consider divorce, especially when there are children in the picture, it may signify that there were irreconcilable differences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Whether this is factual, the Court's assessment of the relationship and further intervention would come in handy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thus, I urge the Government to share more details about the assessment process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it involve professionals in family affairs, such as marriage counsellors, therapists, mediators as well as social workers who work with family and children?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How long would the process take from the time that divorce is filed until there is a conclusion?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the couple appeal if the Court rejects their request for a no-fault divorce?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we can identify potential problems early, couples may be better prepared to deal with them and ameliorate any consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My suggestion is to normalise marriage counselling and make it more accessible to all.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened that many religious leaders have expressed support to help strengthen marital ties and resolve marital disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That said, there remains a stigma among some that seeking counselling is a sign of failure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have a resident who wanted to get marital counselling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, her husband was of the opinion that her concerns are too trivial and that seeing a counsellor was embarrassing and deemed as a waste of time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unfortunately, marital problems may be analogous to cancer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If your signs are not detected and addressed early and when they snowball, the situation becomes implacable or terminal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must do more to destigmatise the shame and trivialisation often associated with marriage problems so that more would take a proactive approach to seek professional help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we expand outreach and improve our family and marriage support services, the demand for resources will grow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do we have sufficiently trained professionals to cater to a projected growing demand?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the average waiting time to seek family counselling under MSF and to get follow-up appointments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under existing policies, there is a mandatory parenting programme for couples with children under 21 years old.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Sweden, a couple filing for divorce may obtain family advice to resolve cohabitation conflicts and, conceivably, avoid divorce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should divorce be inevitable, the family advice service would help to alleviate the conflict to make it possible for the parents to operate together in a parental role.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This service is provided by the municipal and county councils, religious bodies and other private individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to establish that, indeed, the reasons leading to divorce were untenable but mutually agreed – that no one would be held accountable for the divorce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Pre-divorce counselling sessions should involve professionals in relationship and marriage matters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The focus should be on the couple themselves, separate from assets and children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Interactions with the couple during the counselling session would enable professionals to develop a comprehensive assessment on both parties' attitudes and whether there is hope for reconciliation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If, indeed, there is not, they can proceed with counselling on how to move on with childcare, asset division and other implications related to divorce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Couples in a hostile relationship could greatly benefit from professional counselling that is targeted at improving their mental and emotional well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With a healthy mindset, both parties can then work together to seek fairer outcomes from the dissolution of marriage and move on with their lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is with the aim of reversing the breakdown or making the process less acrimonious for all, especially the children, if a dissolution is inevitable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I know of a Mr A who was in an unhappy marriage with his wife.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They had attended marriage counselling but to no avail.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They have children and hope to co-parent them but have some disagreements over shared custody as well as the allocation of assets and resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With appropriate guidance, the estranged couple would, hopefully, come to an agreement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their children would enjoy a healthy childhood under their co-parenting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While it is meaningless to trap people in unhappy marriages, we must continue to encourage the preservation of healthy and happy marriages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Pre-marital counselling is, currently, widely practised and accepted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For religious ceremonies, will the issuers of the certificates be the churches or temples?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not all religious organisations have the digital security resources of Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, I am concerned about the vulnerability of the IT systems.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, I hope the Government can help the religious organisations not only secure digital resources but also ensure safeguards are in place to prevent online theft of these sensitive information.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, under the family tab in Singpass, one can see the marriage certificate number but no indication of the identity of the spouse, which may be important in proving family relationships in emergencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I feel that including a partly-masked name or NRIC number is equally important.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Solemnisers, in journeying with couples in the preparation of the ceremony, very often, become very close friends.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important, therefore, that solemnisers be equipped with counselling skills to help the couples they are marrying.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a previous solemniser myself, some of the couples had turned to me after their weddings for advice when they encountered marital issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I was not trained and could only share my own personal experience.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All families want marriages to work but not all will be able to see them through.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a well-intentioned clause but I am concerned that it could make things worse, especially in marriages where there are children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should be careful about imposing this condition, which might add tension to an already unhappy and strained household.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, the focus in such situations tends to be on helping the younger children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Children mature very quickly these days and young teens can sense what is going on in their parents' relationship.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, they are usually not mature enough to handle all the negative impact and some may even blame themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, urge the Ministry to put more effort to support these children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Engage and counsel them, even the older ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their voices should be heard, and more can be done to ensure that they receive assistance for mental health during and after this very stressful transition period.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   When couples are processing their divorces, the agencies’ focus tends to be on helping the younger children tide over this difficult transition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These days, children mature quite quickly, and young teens can sense what is going wrong in their parents’ relationship.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, they are usually not mature enough to handle all the negative impact by themselves and some may even blame themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Ministry to do its best to support these children, engage and counsel them, even the older ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their feelings and thoughts should also be heard.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry can do more to ensure they receive assistance for mental health during and after this very stressful transition period.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Sir, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In reality, the Charter protects some men, women and children from exploitation within the family.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My colleague, Member of Parliament Louis Ng, spoke on this earlier and I would like to reiterate the same point.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can still do more to promote gender equality and also address the erroneous impression that the Women's Charter protects only women's rights when what it aims to do is to protect the rights of individuals, pertaining to families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My speech will focus on the matters around divorce.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And I speak as someone who had been married before, had an annulment and is currently dating a partner who was divorced with two lovely sons.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And I speak because I believe that we can re-imagine life post-divorce and that second chances can be better.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the spirit of enabling better healing from the pain and trauma of divorce, renaming the Charter would send an important signal to reduce the animosity seen too often in divorce proceedings.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This common misconception that there is a statute that protects women against men, gives divorce a "zero-sum" tone that induces a fear-based and defensive approach.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, the mindset that divorce cases must be "fought", and that someone must win and someone will lose.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In line with making divorces less acrimonious, renaming the Charter to Family Charter can reduce the acrimony and forge a more collaborative approach to negotiating divorce settlements.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The aim of divorce proceedings should and must be to ensure all parties’ well-being post-divorce and not of anyone winning or losing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For that, the spirit of collaboration should and can exist even when someone breaks up, when one seeks to ensure the well-being, especially that of the children’s.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My hon colleague Mr Lim Biow Chuan mentioned earlier a variety of ways children are caught between acts of vengefulness by parents against each other.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With the change in name to Family Charter, no gender’s rights or interest is placed above another's.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Husbands would have less reason to perceive that the system is against them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Defensive or retaliatory behaviours stemming from acrimony, mounted whichever way by husband or wife, can cause undue suffering and, most unfairly, to children who have to witness the ill-feelings between their parents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The emotional trauma and wounds on children from divorce can have long-lasting impact, as an MSF report has shown last year.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Since the intention behind the Charter is to protect people, families and children, the intention must be seen through by taking into account the perceptions that can arise from its name.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the maintenance of children and the ex-spouse, and I believe it should go both ways.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the past, it may have been the predominant phenomenon that men were the primary breadwinners and that women were the primary caregivers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In our current efforts to uplift women and help women fulfil their career aspirations, I have championed the ungendering of care as a key tenet to free up women’s bandwidth from an overburden of care responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As a feminist, I believe there should be no double standards.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If women expect men to pull their weight in domestic and caregiving chores in order to free us up to pursue our career aspirations, it follows logically that in cases where a woman earns much more than her husband and the husband has been taking on more of the domestic responsibilities, husbands should also be able to access maintenance after divorce.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will send a strong signal and provide actual reassurance to men that their well-being and rights, too, are protected should their roles at home be shifted vis-à-vis their wives.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: After all, not only women and girls get hurt.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Men can be victims of violence, too, whether in domestic settings or in wider contexts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have come across cases during my Meet-the-People Sessions where husbands suffer physical abuse from violent wives, as well as mental abuse through emotional blackmail and threats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, these are rarely reported due to the stigma around men showing their vulnerability.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I will share here a quote in Mandarin from one of my residents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: He said: “政府只要保护女人，这个没有错。可是谁会聆听我们的心声。” or “The Government wants to protect the women; it is not wrong.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But who is going to listen to the men's voices?" To truly protect families, men deserve protection equally and clauses should provide for that, even if the number of occurrences of men being victims are significantly lower than women.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: At the risk of sounding utilitarian – and my intention is not to undermine the sanctity of marriage but to take a pragmatic view – we must note that couples are getting married at older ages now, compared to 40 years ago.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Much time is spent and wasted because the current Charter only allows couples to apply for divorce after three years of marriage.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And this is precious time lost for those who find out after getting married and living together that they are not the right lifelong partners for each other.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the perspective that marriages need to be worked at and differences need time to be worked through for marriages to work out, and I agree with Mr Lim Biow Chuan's views that we should not offer an easy cop-out.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are also cases where individuals may find out intolerable issues about their spouses only after marriage, such as chronic infidelity, a tendency towards violence that surfaces only after the honeymoon period, or a history of debilitating financial debt that renders a marriage unreasonably difficult.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Those contemplating divorce while suffering in a marriage would be caught deliberating what would be considered or not considered "exceptional hardship".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What would be helpful would be a non-exhaustive list of factors or considerations of what would constitute exceptional hardship or depravity to serve as a guide for the Courts and also for those experiencing suffering within their marriages within the first three years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In cases where the individuals in the marriage have irreconcilable differences, a three-year window of futile attempts at reconciliation is precious time lost that holds individuals back from pursuing a more fulfilled life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I recognise that it is a difficult matter to choose and decide on, whether we should mandate time for the couples to work things out in order to "save marriages" or allow people to move on and to pursue the possibility of more workable marriages.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Some data would be helpful, and we should look into data on how successful the deed of separation has been in achieving reconciliation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What numbers of marriages get successfully salvaged and turned around after the deed of separation period?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hopefully, the couple can channel most of their energy and resources to moving forward or, in the case where there are children, making suitable new arrangements to care for them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that this section may even be a lifesaver in preventing some couples' situations from escalating, which could, potentially, cause harm to themselves or their children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The process of separating and breaking up a family is so stressful and emotional.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There had been cases in the past where one or both parties inflict physical harm on each other or their kids.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Ministry must continue to review our measures to deter those who want to marry for convenience.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The penalties must be suitably set at levels which will be effective deterrents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would, first, like to declare that I am a practising lawyer and a member of the Law Society's Family Law Committee 2022.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: According to the Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale, divorce is one of the most stressful events in one's life, second only to the death of a loved one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This finding is unsurprising as part of the divorce process involves parties coming before the Family Court to end their marriage and address how their most private family affairs will be restructured.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More often than not, the contentious divorce proceedings can prove to be emotionally-charged events for embroiled parties, overriding rational thinking and clouding judgements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unfortunately, the children are usually not spared from the effects and stresses of their parents' divorce, even though they are the most innocent parties in these matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are ways to make the entire divorce process less strenuous and minimally impactful for our little ones if everyone is on the same page.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As what the Presiding Judge of the Family Justice Courts, Justice Debbie Ong, has shared in her workplan speech in 2020, the Family Justice Courts and the Family Justice Community will be co-creating a renewed vision of family justice, informed by the principles of therapeutic justice.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is the hope that our collective efforts would help to engender a mindset shift in the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The resolution of family disputes need not be an adversarial one but should be focused on solutions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, speak in support of this amendment Bill as I am hopeful that several of the changes that will be brought about by the passing of this Bill would encourage parties to work out their marital differences, lessen the acrimony of Court proceedings and foster parties' cooperation towards co-parenting their children post-divorce.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will be beneficial to the affected children as studies have shown that the level of acrimony during a divorce proceeding has a perceptible impact on a child's well-being.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children should not be expected to take sides and be caught in a conflict of loyalty.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead, they should continue to be embraced by both parents with love and attention, regardless of their respective marital status.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: John Bowlby's Attachment Theory asserts the notions that children need warm, consistent and responsive caregivers to form secure attachments.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Interruptions and interferences in the attachment-formation years can have long-lasting impact resulting in insecure attachment styles.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We often hear of stories of parental alienation, where a parent would refuse the other party from having access to the child as a result of hatred, or as a retaliation to deprivation of maintenance by the other party.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are also situations where the child has rejected one parent's request for contact so as to appease the other parent whom they are residing with.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that these sessions will take place at the Divorce Support Specialist Agencies (DSSAs).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I wish to seek clarifications on whether there are any fees applicable and payable by parties for participation in such sessions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, the supervised exchange or supervised visitation programmes ordered by the Court to take place at DSSAs are free of charge for the first three Court orders.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From the fourth Court order onwards, however, the parties will have to pay for such services at DSSAs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are, presently, seven family service centres and DSSAs located across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In view of the increased support, would the Ministry consider increasing the number of complimentary sessions for parties to carry out supervised access at the DSSAs?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would the social service agencies also be able to provide more hand-holding services to closely monitor the education and welfare of the children during and after their parents' divorce so as to prevent the possibility of delinquency and other potential social complications?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As what Mr Lim Biow Chuan has shared earlier in his speech, in order to file for divorce in Singapore, one has to, first, persuade the Court that the marriage has irretrievably broken down by citing one of the facts, either fault-based or non-fault-based, as set out in section 95A of the Women's Charter.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, parties who are unable to fulfil the requirements to file for divorce based on the non-fault-based facts are, nevertheless, required to cite facts blaming the other spouse as the cause of the breakdown of the marriage even when both are cordial about ending the marriage in the first place.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the new fact, couples are to take joint responsibility for the breakdown of the marriage and will have to include, among other reasons, the reasons for the marital breakdown in their submissions to the Court.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I hope the Ministry can elaborate on what types of reasons are deemed as acceptable to substantiate that the marriage has irretrievably broken down under the new sixth fact.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I understand that the Minister of State has shared earlier that parties may cite examples of their deep-seated differences so as to substantiate this fact.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I hope that the particulars to be mentioned to support this fact need not require parties to set out each other's misdeeds as that will require them to rehash their marital disputes all over again.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my opinion, this does not assist in reducing the acrimony between the parties.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Moreover, I do hope that parties should avoid attributing the children as the reason for the breakdown of the marriage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children should not be made to feel that they are the cause of their parents' divorce.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As mentioned earlier, divorce does have long-term effects on children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Social science research has shown that feelings of guilt, abandonment and shame have adverse impact on a child's physical and mental health development.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I support the inclusion of this requirement, especially when children are involved.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the Family Justice Practice Forum 2020, Miss Audrey Siew, then director of the Family Support Division of MSF, shared that an intergenerational study was conducted in 2020 to examine the long-term impact of divorce on children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from illustrating the reconciliation efforts, the parties will also need to set out the considerations that they have made for their children and the financial affairs in their submissions to the Court when filing under the sixth fact.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are situations where a divorce filed in an acrimonious manner, for example, on the basis of the defendant's unreasonable behaviour or adultery, has since seen both parties subsequently undergo mediation at the Family Justice Courts, during which marital reconciliation was explored, but failed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, these parties have, in turn, reached an amicable global settlement on the divorce and ancillaries through mediation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a Chinese saying: 家家有本难念的经 — every family has its own challenges.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Families which are involved in litigation often come with complex needs and issues.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Underlying many of these family disputes are non-legal-related concerns.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As such, I echo the need for collaborative, holistic and multidisciplinary interventions to be used to address the families' underlying dysfunctions and emotional needs whenever possible.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More importantly, we should prevent the children from feeling distressed while in the midst of their parents' divorce proceedings, bearing in mind that such an adverse experience can have a lasting negative impact on their lives, lasting far into adulthood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In essence, however, it can be argued that DMA makes the divorce process easier.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I was taught that marriages are meant to be sacred and lasting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The divorce process should not be made too easy as we want couples to work through their problems that will, inevitably, crop up in any marriage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Major challenges, such as struggling to care for their first-born who refuses to stop crying in the middle of the night or coping with the financial squeeze that couples with young children and elderly parents to care for, are par for the course.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These are everyday marital problems, and we should provide couples with the tools to resolve communication issues, instead of making divorce a simple, straightforward, easy solution.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, as a grassroots leader and former Police officer, I have also seen cases of how being trapped in an unhappy marriage can be damaging on a person's well-being – emotionally, mentally and, at times, even physically.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That is why, despite my personal view on marriage, I can understand and appreciate the reason for the introduction of DMA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But that being said, we should do more to intervene upstream to help strengthen marriages, so that we can prevent relationships from deteriorating to the point where couples have to contemplate divorce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, MSF could make marriage preparation courses more extensive and, I would even argue, mandatory.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Before I got married, my wife-to-be and I had to attend the Marriage Preparation Course conducted by the Church.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The course, which comprised six sessions, taught us the fundamentals of a healthy marriage and equipped us with tools to work out our differences in a constructive way.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While there are marriage preparation programmes on the market, most seem to emphasise on how couples can be equipped with the right tools in as little time as possible, with some courses taking just two weekends.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I wonder if this is truly sufficient to prepare two distinct individuals to live together for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Currently, MSF only mandates marriage preparation courses if the marriage involves someone below the age of 21.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would suggest that a comprehensive marriage preparation programme be put together and for marrying couples of all ages to be strongly encouraged to participate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many of us go for a regular health check-up, sometimes yearly, sometimes once every two years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Why not have a regular check-up for our marriages, too?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is it linked to certain key life moments that changed the dynamics of the relationship?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that MSF could make marriage therapy more affordable and accessible, so that we can help couples take stock of their relationships and strengthen their marriages.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And this could be done through mandatory pre-divorce counselling programmes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Currently, pre-divorce counselling is only mandatory for parents with minor children before they file for divorce and is designed to encourage divorcing couples to make informed decisions to prioritise the well-being of their children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In cases where the wife was a homemaker, it can be difficult for them to re-enter the workforce easily as their skillsets may not be updated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In this regard, NTUC has been working with our affiliated unions, the Employment and Employability Institute and NTUC Learning Hub, to support single mothers by bringing employment and training opportunities to them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I encourage all single mums who need help returning to the workplace to turn to the Labour Movement for support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Single mothers also have less familial support when it comes to caregiving and will require more support in helping them balance their careers and caregiving duties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Radin Mas, we partnered Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF) to launch the Jobs Closer to Home Programme in 2021 to help mothers with caregiving responsibilities find jobs that are closer to home, so that they can balance work and their roles as a mother and caregiver.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This has helped some single mothers in my constituency to gain meaningful employment and I hope this can be scaled up nationally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to call on Action for Alliance on Work-Life Harmony to look at how companies can implement more flexible work arrangements specifically catered to single parents, so that we can help them to be the best parent that they can be to their children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
